cim: Az újabb AI-bumm ingatlanpiaci válsággal fenyegeti San Franciscót
lead: Az OpenAI és az Anthropic dolgozóinak részvényvagyona drasztikusan felverheti a San Francisco-i ingatlanárakat a helyi dolgozók szerint.
osszefoglalo:
A San Francisco-öböl térségében jelentős vagyoni növekedést hoz a magántulajdonú AI-cégek szárnyalása, ami újabb lakhatási megélhetési válságot idézhet elő. A Redfin elemzése szerint az **OpenAI és az Anthropic** jelenlegi és korábbi munkavállalói együttesen közel 200 milliárd dolláros adózott részvényvagyon felett rendelkezhetnek a jelenlegi cégértékelések alapján.

Ez a becsült vagyon a San Francisco-i agglomeráció teljes lakóingatlan-értékének nagyjából **29 százalékának felel meg**. Bár a helyi technológiai szektor dolgozói korábban a magas ingatlanárak nyerteseinek számítottak, sokan közülük attól tartanak, hogy az elszabaduló árak miatt kénytelenek lesznek elköltözni a régióból.
miert_szamit: A hír elsősorban regionális **ingatlanpiaci és gazdasági folyamatokat** mutat be, közvetlen hatása nincs a hazai AI-eszközök mindennapi használatára.

cim_eredeti: Artificial Intelligence: AI boom brings new wealth to Bay Area, and new worries about growing affordability crisis
szoveg_eredeti:
SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- Jennifer Lum has a good job in tech, a two-year-old and a front-row seat to the extraordinary wealth being created by the artificial intelligence boom.

But like many working people across the Bay Area, she's thinking carefully about what the region's next chapter could mean for her family.

"We have a unique housing situation that allows us to live here," said Lum, a senior account executive at Slack Salesforce. "But if it were to fall through, I could see us having to move."

That tension was difficult to miss at Dreamforce, Salesforce's annual conference in San Francisco that was held this month -- where artificial intelligence dominated conversations about the future of work and technology.

EXCLUSIVE: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff touts AI for all as Dreamforce returns to San Francisco

Outside the conference halls, another transformation is unfolding alongside it.

The Bay Area is bracing for a potentially enormous influx of wealth tied to private AI companies. Redfin estimates current and former OpenAI and Anthropic employees hold nearly $200 billion in after-tax equity at the company valuations modeled in its analysis. That estimated wealth is equivalent to roughly 29% of the value of all residential real estate in the San Francisco metro area, according to Redin's analysis.

The comparison is illustrative, not a prediction that AI employees will buy anything close to that share of the region's homes. But Lum said she is already seeing the effects of private tech wealth firsthand.

"I'm also seeing people buying houses with pre-IPO stock," she said. "So it's going to get interesting."

MORE: Buying homes with pre-IPO OpenAI stock? New trend going viral in San Francisco

For a region that has lived through multiple technology booms, the dynamic is a familiar one: enormous new wealth arriving in a place where housing was already scarce and expensive.

Jesus Oroseo remembers the last time it happened.

As a Bay Area native and longtime software developer at Salesforce, he lived through the dot-com boom and bust. He sees similarities in the frenzy surrounding AI, though he remains relatively sanguine about the technology itself.

"There's been a lot of craziness then and it seems like it's happening again," Oroseo said. "We're going to get through this, and we're going to come out on the other side."

His concern is less about whether AI survives the hype cycle than what happens to the people trying to live alongside it.

MORE: AI IPO boom set to transform San Francisco, starting with soaring real estate prices

Oroseo bought his Fremont home about 25 years ago, a decision that now puts him in a dramatically different position from younger workers trying to enter the Bay Area housing market.

"I'm on the lucky side," he said. "I just wonder how people can make it with those kind of prices."

"There's people who can't make it or it's just too expensive to make it," Oroseo said. "And I've had some friends who have packed up and left."

That experience complicates a familiar image of the Bay Area's affordability crisis, one that places highly paid tech workers exclusively on the winning side of rising housing costs.

MORE: 'A million dollars over asking': AI wealth is fueling housing market frenzy in San Francisco

Oroseo doesn't describe himself as financially struggling.

"I'm certainly not underpaid by any means," he said. "And it gets tough."

He is a Salesforce software engineer in his 20s and the most unabashedly optimistic of the three workers ABC7 News interviewed at Dreamforce. "I don't really buy the whole doomsday stuff," he said. "It feels like a lot of fun. We're helping people."
